transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Giles Snyder.
Nearly 30 tech executives from NVIDIA, OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic gathered at the White
House Tuesday for a meeting on artificial intelligence.
NPR's Emily Fang reports that many of the executives present have conflicting views
on the mounting concerns about the safety of the technology.
Rather than settle on what should be regulated, President Trump said the meeting leaned towards
letting the AI companies regulate themselves.
There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation, and we automatically have
regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that.
Of course, regulators have to make rules before prosecutors can enforce them.
Trump also said they discuss tech companies helping local communities more when they build
data centers.
That might be supplying oil and gas, it might be supplying education.
Data centers are unpopular among the American electorate, but Trump is a strong supporter
of them.
Emily Fang, NPR News, The White House.
Following the meeting, Trump unveiled a one-page document on social media that he said is a
voluntary accord with major tech companies on AI.
He said they have agreed to police themselves amid calls for the government to establish
guardrails.
New York Democratic Senator Kirsten Gillibrand is calling on Congress to act after prosecutors
this week reopened an investigation into an alleged gang rape at a Cornell University
frat house.
I do imagine that many campuses have put in place much better policies than they had a
decade ago, but Congress hasn't done its part, and we just spent two weeks talking about
college sports.
Congress should spend at least that time talking about how to make campuses safe for all students.
Prosecutors reopened the case after the alleged victim filed a civil lawsuit against Cornell
and seven students accused of taking part in the assault.
New York Governor Kathy Hogle is calling for an independent investigation, saying the case
raises serious questions about Cornell's campus culture.
The CDC has added a second measles death to its national tally this year.
It comes after Pennsylvania reported four deaths linked to measles.
Here's NPR's Maria Godoy.
The CDC website did not identify where the death occurred, so it's unclear if the new
death is one of the four reported in Pennsylvania.
No other state has reported a measles-associated death this year.
The deaths have become wrapped up in a political feud between Pennsylvania's Democratic Governor
Josh Shapiro and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
When Shapiro announced the first two deaths, Kennedy initially questioned whether they were
due to measles, and in a highly unusual move, the CDC initially excluded them from its weekly
measles tally.
The CDC says it's working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to
develop a standardized definition for deaths due to measles.
Maria Godoy, NPR News.
And from Washington, you're listening to NPR News.
Several defendants in the alleged cocaine trafficking ring at Penn State say they plan
to plead not guilty.
Sydney Roach of member station WPSU has more on the latest developments.
Five of the people named in the investigation, including the alleged ring leaders, were originally
scheduled for formal arraignments on Wednesday, but court officials say those defendants have
waived formal arraignments.
They'll be back in court in November, and both of the alleged ring leaders are requesting
a jury trial.
Thirteen former Penn State students and one of their parents were arrested last month before
the start of the current fall semester.
India's attorney general says cocaine packaging and sales allegedly happened at two off-campus
fraternity houses from 2023 to 2024.
For NPR News, I'm Sydney Roach in State College, Pennsylvania.
A former American Idol contestant has been convicted of murder and the killing of his
wife.
A Miami County, Ohio jury found Caleb Flynn guilty on Tuesday.
Prosecutors allege Flynn staged a home invasion in February after shooting his wife.
He claims she was killed by a burglar.
He is to be sentenced on Monday and could get up to life in prison without the chance
of parole.
National Hurricane Center in Miami expected Tropical Storm Rachel is expecting Tropical
Storm Rachel to strengthen into a hurricane soon.
Rachel is moving parallel to Mexico's southwestern coast.
It's expected to stay offshore.
Meanwhile, the remnants of Hurricane Polo moving into the southwestern U.S., compounding
flood worries and leading to evacuation orders in three small towns in New Mexico.
I'm Giles Snyder, NPR News.
